content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 12: Database and Server-Side Injection Vulnerabilities. It builds practical understanding of SQL Injection Fundamentals with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: SQL Injection Fundamentals addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Use parameterized queries or safe ORM APIs so user-controlled values remain data, then add regression tests and restrict database privileges.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: SQL Injection Fundamentals can be understood through this sequence: Receive untrusted data → Keep data separate → Validate safe interface → Regression test. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 84.1 SQL parsing and query construction; 84.2 Trusted code versus untrusted data; 84.3 Injection risks in read and write operations; 84.4 Potential database and application impact; 84.5 Identifying unsafe query patterns in code. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Use parameterized queries or safe ORM APIs so user-controlled values remain data, then add regression tests and restrict database privileges.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: SQL Injection Fundamentals
content_blocks.code:
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE users (email TEXT)")
email = "student@example.test"  # treat this as untrusted input
rows = connection.execute(
    "SELECT email FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,)
).fetchall()
print(rows)
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as a Python script and run with Python 3. The `?` placeholder binds the value separately from SQL syntax; do not interpolate input into the query string.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Use parameterized queries or safe ORM APIs so user-controlled values remain data, then add regression tests and restrict database privileges. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “SQL Injection Fundamentals”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for SQL Injection Fundamentals in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.

Use parameterized queries or safe ORM APIs so user-controlled values remain data, then add regression tests and restrict database privileges.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
